entry: Figure in the [[Hebrew Bible]] and [[Abrahamic religions]]. She is first mentioned there, where she brings a caravan of valuable gifts to [[Solomon]], fourth King of Israel and Judah. Her name is given as Bilqis in Arabic and Makeda in Geʽez. The story was elaborated in [[Judaism]], Ethiopian Christianity and [[Islam]]. Historians identify [[Sheba]] as a South Arabian kingdom in modern-day [[Yemen]], but no trace of the queen has been found, and her existence is disputed.

Borough of [[New York City]] (pop., 2020: 2,405,464), coextensive with Queens County. It is the largest of the five boroughs by area and lies near the western end of [[Long Island]], bordered by [[Brooklyn]] to the west. About 47% of its residents are foreign-born. Queens County was established in 1683, and the borough was created in 1898 during the consolidation of New York City. It is home to [[John F. Kennedy International Airport|John F. Kennedy]] and LaGuardia airports, and to the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, site of the U.S. Open tennis tournament.

State of northeastern [[Australia]], with an area of 1,723,030 sq km. Its capital and largest city is [[Brisbane]]. The area was first inhabited by [[Aboriginal Australians]]. In 1770, [[James Cook]] claimed the east coast for Britain, and the region remained part of [[New South Wales]] until June 6, 1859, when Queen Victoria signed letters patent establishing the separate colony of Queensland. It became one of the six founding states of Australia on January 1, 1901. Its economy has strengths in mining, agriculture and tourism, and it is nicknamed the Sunshine State.

American filmmaker, actor and author. His works are characterized by graphic violence, extended dialogue, [[Profanity|profanity]] and references to [[Popular culture|popular culture]]. His debut feature, the independent crime film *Reservoir Dogs* (1992), was an immediate hit. *Pulp Fiction* (1994) won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] and his first [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]], for Best Original Screenplay, and it was inducted into the National Film Registry of the [[Library of Congress]]. *Kill Bill: Volume 1* (2003) and *Kill Bill: Volume 2* (2004) are regarded as a single film. *Django Unchained* (2012) won him a second Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay, and his later films include *Inglourious Basterds* (2009) and *The Hateful Eight* (2015). His films have grossed more than $1.9 billion worldwide.

Utterance that serves as a request for [[Information|information]]. Questions are distinct from interrogatives, the grammatical forms typically used to express them. Polar questions can be answered with "yes" or "no", alternative questions present a list of possibilities, and open questions allow many possible answers. Rhetorical questions are interrogative in form but are not expected to be answered. Questions are widely studied in [[Linguistics]] and [[Philosophy of language|philosophy of language]]. In [[Pragmatics|pragmatics]], questions are regarded as illocutionary acts that raise an issue to be resolved in discourse. In approaches to [[Semantics|formal semantics]], questions are identified with sets of the propositions that answer them. Questions can also serve as indirect speech acts, such as requests for action phrased as interrogatives.

Deity in [[Aztecs|Aztec]] culture and literature. Among the Aztecs he was related to wind, the planet [[Venus]], the Sun, merchants, arts, crafts, knowledge and learning, and he was patron god of the priesthood. He was one of several important gods in the Aztec pantheon, along with Tlaloc, Tezcatlipoca and Huitzilopochtli. The name comes from Nahuatl and means "Precious serpent" or "Quetzal-feathered Serpent." The earliest known documentation of the worship of a Feathered Serpent is from [[Teotihuacan]] in the first century BC or first century AD, and veneration spread through [[Mesoamerica]] by the Late Classic period (AD 600–900). In records written after the 16th-century Spanish conquest, he was conflated with the Toltec ruler Ce Acatl Topiltzin, although historians debate whether those narratives describe real events. Early Spanish clerics identified him with [[Hernán Cortés]] or Thomas the Apostle.

Genus of azhdarchid [[Pterosaur|pterosaurs]] from the Late Cretaceous of North America. Its type specimen was found in 1971 in the Javelina Formation of [[Texas]] and was described in 1975 by Douglas Lawson as *Quetzalcoatlus northropi*. The genus name refers to the Aztec serpent god, and the species name honors aviation pioneer Jack Northrop. The species is a candidate for the largest flying animal ever discovered, with estimates of 10–11 m (33–36 ft) in wingspan. Later research suggests it hunted small prey on the ground, similar to storks and ground hornbills.

Most populous city in the [[Philippines]], in [[Metro Manila]] (pop., 2024: 3,084,270). Named after Manuel L. Quezon, the second president of the Philippines, it was founded on October 12, 1939, and was intended to replace [[Manila]] as the national capital, which was suffering from overcrowding and traffic congestion. It served as the capital from 1948 until 1976, when Presidential Decree No. 940 returned that status to Manila. It is a planned city and the largest in Metro Manila by land area, covering 161.11 sq km with 142 barangays. Known as the "City of Stars" for its entertainment industry and broadcasting networks, it is home to the Batasang Pambansa Complex, seat of the House of Representatives. Its northern part lies at the foothills of the Sierra Madre, including the La Mesa Watershed Reservation.

Divide-and-conquer [[Sorting algorithm|sorting algorithm]] developed by British computer scientist Tony Hoare in 1959 and published in 1961. It selects a pivot element, partitions the other elements into sub-arrays of lesser and greater values, and sorts those recursively. On average, it takes O(n log n) comparisons to sort n items, but O(n²) in the worst case. Most implementations are not stable, and on randomized data it is slightly faster than merge sort and heapsort. It was widely adopted, appearing as the default library sort in [[Unix]].

Deciduous tree (*Cydonia oblonga*) of the [[Rosaceae|rose family]], bearing hard, aromatic golden-yellow pome fruit similar in appearance to a pear. The ripe fruit is tart and astringent and is eaten raw or processed into jam, quince cheese or alcoholic drinks. Native to the Hyrcanian forests south of the [[Caspian Sea]] in Iran, quince was spread by Neolithic farmers, c. 5000 to 3000 BC. The tree is also grown as an ornamental for its pale pink blossoms. Its seeds contain nitriles that yield toxic [[Hydrogen cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]] in the stomach, but they are toxic only if eaten in large quantities.

Coming-of-age celebration of a girl's 15th birthday in [[Latin America|Latin American]] cultures. Practices vary and can take on religious overtones, but typically involve food, dancing, music and the girl of honor wearing a tiara. Contemporary festivities combine Catholic traditions from old Spain with indigenous heritage of pre-Columbian Mexico. In rural societies, girls were considered ready for marriage at 15. The celebration was reinforced during the Second Mexican Empire, when Empress Carlota held a similar reception for her court in [[Mexico City]].

American record producer, musician and composer. Over a seven-decade career, he received dozens of honors, including 28 [[Grammy Awards]]. He produced three of [[Michael Jackson]]'s most successful albums, *Off the Wall* (1979), *Thriller* (1982) and *Bad* (1987), and in 1985 he produced and conducted a charity song that raised funds for famine victims in Ethiopia. Jones came to prominence as a [[Jazz|jazz]] arranger and conductor in the 1950s and composed film scores including *In the Heat of the Night* (1967). He also received a Tony Award for Best Revival of a Musical, as a producer of the 2016 revival of *The Color Purple*.

Alkaloid used medically to treat [[Malaria|malaria]] and babesiosis. It was first isolated in 1820 from the bark of a cinchona tree native to [[Peru]], and bark extracts had been used against malaria since at least 1632. [[Jesuits|Jesuit]] missionaries introduced it to Spain in 1636. Treatment of malaria with quinine marks the first known use of a chemical compound against an infectious disease, and quinine is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines. As of 2006, the organization no longer recommended it as a first-line treatment for malaria, advising its use only when artemisinins are not available. Common side effects include headache, [[Tinnitus|ringing in the ears]], vision problems and sweating. Quinine is also a flavor component of tonic water, which, according to tradition, British colonials in India mixed with gin to make the gin and tonic cocktail.

Annual plant of the [[Amaranth|amaranth]] family, *Chenopodium quinoa*, grown primarily for its edible seeds. It is a pseudocereal botanically related to spinach and amaranth rather than a grass, and it originated in the [[Andes|Andean]] region of northwestern South America. It was first used to feed livestock 5,200–7,000 years ago and for human consumption 3,000–4,000 years ago in the [[Lake Titicaca]] basin of Bolivia and Peru. The seeds are high in protein, dietary fiber, B vitamins, potassium and magnesium. Cultivation has spread to more than 70 countries, and as consumption rose in North America, Europe and Australasia, quinoa crop prices tripled between 2006 and 2014. The [[United Nations]] designated 2013 as the International Year of Quinoa.

Capital of [[Ecuador]] and of Pichincha province, in the [[Andes]]. It is the country's political and cultural center and its second-largest city after [[Guayaquil]], with an estimated 1.7 million people in the city and 2.8 million in its metropolitan area. At 2,850 meters (9,350 ft), Quito is either the highest or second-highest national capital in the world. Archaeological evidence suggests that it was first settled between 4400 and 1600 BC. The [[Inca Empire]] incorporated it in the late 15th century, and the Spanish conquest in 1534 is the date most often cited as its official founding, making Quito the oldest capital in South America. Its historic center, one of the largest and best-preserved in the Americas, was among the first sites declared a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site, in 1978, together with [[Kraków]].

Form of mind sport in which people attempt to answer questions correctly on one or several topics. Quizzes are used as brief assessments in education and similar fields, or simply as a [[Hobby|hobby]]. They are often televised for entertainment in a [[Game show|game show]] format. In education, a quiz usually has fewer questions, of less difficulty, than a test. The earliest known examples of the word date to 1780. A well-known myth credits a [[Dublin]] theatre owner, Richard Daly, with popularizing it through a bet in 1791, but there is no evidence for the story, since the word was already in use. Popular competitive formats include pub quizzes and quiz bowl. The largest quiz recorded by the Guinness Book of World Records took place in Maihar, India, on June 18, 2017, with 4,900 participants.

Small macropod [[Marsupial|marsupial]] of southwestern [[Australia]]. It is about the size of a domestic [[Cat|cat]], herbivorous and mainly nocturnal. Its range is a small area of [[Western Australia]], including islands such as Rottnest Island just off [[Perth]]. The name derives from a Noongar word. In 1696, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh mistook quokkas for giant rats and renamed the island 't Rottenest, meaning "the rat nest island" in Dutch.

Punctuation mark, used in pairs, to identify direct speech, a quotation or a [[Phrase|phrase]]. The single quotation mark is traced to ancient Greek practice, adopted and adapted by monastic copyists. The double quotation mark derives from a marginal notation in 15th-century manuscripts that marked passages of particular importance. In his 1483 or 1484 edition of [[Aristotle]], the Milanese humanist Francesco Filelfo marked literal quotations in the margin, and quotation marks for literal quotations prevailed. By the 19th century, designs varied by region: in Britain the marks were raised to the height of capital letters, and in France they became angular.

sort_key: quotations from chairman mao tse tung
entry: Compilation of speeches and writings by [[Mao Zedong]], chairman of the [[Chinese Communist Party]], published 1964–79 and known as the *Little Red Book*. It was originally compiled by an office of the *PLA Daily* as an ideological handbook. The first internal edition was released in May 1964 by the General Political Department of the [[People's Liberation Army]]. The definitive 1965 version contained 33 thematic chapters with 427 quotations drawn from Mao's writings between 1929 and 1964. From 1966 the book was printed by the People's Publishing House and widely distributed during the [[Cultural Revolution]]. Estimates of copies printed range from 800 million to over 5 billion worldwide.

Additive color model in which red, green and blue light are added together in various ways to reproduce a broad array of colors. It is used mainly for the sensing, representation and display of images in electronic systems such as televisions and computers. Mixing all three primaries at full intensity produces white, and equal intensities produce shades of gray. Because the phosphors, dyes and display elements of devices vary, an RGB value does not define the same color across devices without color management. Color printers, by contrast, are subtractive devices that typically use the [[CMYK color model]]. The sRGB variant uses 8 bits per channel, allowing 16.7 million possible colors.

Family of public-key cryptosystems, one of the oldest, widely used for secure data transmission. The name comes from Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, who publicly described the algorithm in 1977 while at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. An equivalent system was developed secretly in 1973 at GCHQ, the British signals intelligence agency, by Clifford Cocks, and was declassified in 1997. The private key is a pair of large [[Prime number|prime numbers]], and the public key is their product. Security depends on the difficulty of factoring that product.

American rock band formed in Athens, Georgia, in 1980. Its members were Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe. Buck's arpeggiated guitar and Stipe's cryptic lyrics were distinctive, and later [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] acts named the band a pioneer of the genre. *Out of Time* (1991) and *Automatic for the People* (1992) were its most commercially successful albums, and "Losing My Religion" was its highest-charting single. The band broke up amicably in 2011 after selling more than 90 million albums worldwide. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2007, in its first year of eligibility.

American former singer, songwriter and record producer. Born on the South Side of [[Chicago]], Illinois, he achieved commercial success in R&B, [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] and [[Pop music|pop]] and sold over 75 million albums and singles worldwide. His songwriting and production were credited on albums by [[Michael Jackson]] and [[Whitney Houston]]. He was prosecuted on child pornography charges in 2002 and acquitted on all charges in 2008. Convictions in 2021 and 2022 for child sexual abuse and sex trafficking led to a combined 31-year prison sentence.

American novelist, writer of the *Goosebumps* horror series for children. The series has sold over 400 million copies in 35 languages, making it the second-best-selling book series in history, and it spawned a media franchise including television series and films. Stine also wrote the teen horror series *Fear Street*, which has sold over 80 million copies. He has been called the "[[Stephen King]] of [[Children's literature|children's literature]]." Earlier, he created the humor magazine *Bananas* and wrote humor books under the alias Jovial Bob Stine.

Estuary on the southeastern coast of [[South America]], formed where the [[Uruguay River|Uruguay]] and [[Paraná River|Paraná]] rivers meet at Punta Gorda. Depending on the geographer, it may be considered a river, an estuary, a gulf or a marginal sea. If considered a river, it is the widest in the world, with a maximum width of 220 km. It is about 290 km long and forms part of the border between [[Argentina]] and Uruguay. The name, meaning "River of Silver," reflects a myth that the region held vast amounts of silver, which is also why the country is named Argentina, meaning loosely "silvery land." The coasts are the most densely populated areas of Uruguay and Argentina, and the port cities of [[Buenos Aires]] and [[Montevideo]] are where Rioplatense Spanish and [[Tango|tango]] culture developed.
